claims.text: MLLMs struggle with fine-grained pixel understanding, while VQA and visual grounding do not effectively assess this capability.
HLMAT models interactive segmentation as a multi-step Markov Decision Process in which MLLMs generate text-based coordinates without specialized architectures or implicit tokens.

SegAgent receives the current mask overlaid on the image and a task and object description, then outputs a textual click action; an interactive segmentation model uses the action history, current mask and image to update the mask.

Training trajectories are simulated from ground-truth masks by placing clicks in false-positive or false-negative regions; generation limits trajectory length, stops at a reward threshold and discards actions below a reward-improvement threshold.

StaR+ retains rollout actions that increase reward, replaces reward-decreasing actions with simulator corrections, and fine-tunes on the corrected trajectories merged with the original trajectory dataset.

At inference, the MLLM predicts the current mask's mIoU as a process reward. Heuristic greedy search samples K candidate actions, evaluates their resulting masks using PRM, selects the highest predicted reward and returns the mask with the highest predicted reward across steps.
RES comprises refCOCO, refCOCO+ and refCOCOg. HRES derives from HQSeg-44K using DIS5K and ThinObject5K; DIS5K contains 5,470 images across 22 groups and 225 fine-grained categories.
Evaluation uses cumulative IoU, with maximum steps T=7 and K=1 for RES, and T=11 and K=3 for HRES.
On refCOCO validation, SegAgent-LLaVA+SAM scores 79.20 compared with 71.79 for Qwen box + SAM; on refCOCOg test(U), the corresponding scores are 74.90 and 68.94.

A single round of StaR+ yields ThinObject5K IoU of 86.57 compared with the SFT baseline's 71.45. PRM alone improves performance by 2.36 on DIS and 4.09 on ThinObject; search with K=3 adds 7.43 and 10.59, respectively, over PRM alone.
For annotation filtering, SegAgent-LLaVA has MAE 5.58, MSE 175.35, Pearson correlation 0.91 and Spearman correlation 0.90; SegAgent-Qwen has 6.88, 193.98, 0.90 and 0.87, respectively.

Failures mainly involve incorrect initial target localization or inaccurate refinement coordinates, particularly points falling outside object boundaries. The authors consider fine-grained pixel localization the principal performance bottleneck.

Nearly optimal simulated trajectories lack diversity, constraining model generalization and robustness; noisy ground-truth masks can also produce erroneous training actions, especially near trajectory endpoints.
More complex search strategies involve a computational complexity–performance trade-off; exploration of BFS and MCTS is left for future work.

The work introduces HLMAT as a protocol for fine-grained visual capability assessment, SegAgent trained on automatically generated human-like annotation trajectories, and HRES for studying complex vision-centered multi-step decisions.
